# Performance Specification

## Purpose

SortAlgorithms is both an algorithm study library and a performance-oriented implementation. Performance is part of the design contract: hot paths are shaped for the .NET JIT, memory traffic and allocation are controlled, and algorithm variants may deliberately trade code size or predictable-input speed for lower branch-misprediction cost.

Correctness, comparer semantics, observation accuracy, and memory safety take precedence over speed. An optimization is retained only when its applicable input class and trade-offs are understood.

## Runtime Scope

Generated code depends on the runtime, JIT, build configuration, element type, comparer, context, and CPU. Runtime upgrades require revalidation of claims that depend on instruction selection or crossover points. Measurements and implementation decisions are kept in [reports](../reports/README.md), separately from this contract.

## Execution Modes

### Unobserved sorting

The ordinary overloads use the value-type `NullContext`. `TContext` remains generic throughout `SortSpan<T, TComparer, TContext>` and algorithm helpers, and hot operations branch on the closed generic type. For a `NullContext` specialization, the JIT can constant-fold the type test and remove callback and statistics paths.

"Zero-cost statistics" means that selecting `NullContext` does not execute observation callbacks or maintain counters. It does not promise identical code size or instruction layout on every .NET/JIT version; generated-code claims are checked with disassembly.

The theoretical basis is closed-generic specialization. `NullContext` is a value type, so the JIT sees a concrete `TContext` instantiation rather than a shared interface object. In that instantiation, `typeof(TContext) != typeof(NullContext)` is a compile-time-constant false condition; dead-code elimination can remove the callback arm, its arguments, and counter-related work. Keeping `TContext` generic through every helper is essential: converting it to `ISortContext` would reintroduce interface dispatch and prevent the same whole-path elimination. Disassembly validation checks the closed `NullContext` path for absence of context callback calls and tracking branches rather than inferring zero cost from source syntax.

### Instrumented sorting

A real `TContext` receives the callbacks defined by [observation.md](observation.md). Instrumentation necessarily performs more work, but the built-in statistics path avoids unnecessary synchronization:

- `StatisticsContext` uses ordinary `++`/`+=`, not `Interlocked.Increment`;
- a statistics instance belongs to one sort, or one thread, and must not be shared by concurrent sorts; and
- swaps and range copies update aggregate counters directly rather than replaying individual callback operations.


### Statistics ownership

Sorting is synchronous. A StatisticsContext has one owner during a sort and does not support concurrent mutation. Atomic updates provide no additional correctness under this ownership model. Adding internal parallelism must not silently reuse the current context.

One logical swap updates the swap count and accounts for two reads and two writes. Counter implementation changes must preserve those values. Historical atomic-counter measurements are retained in the [performance evidence record](../reports/performance-evidence-before-f03-2026-11-15.md).

## Implemented Runtime-Level Optimizations

| Area | Adopted design | Why it exists | Constraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Contiguous input | Algorithms sort `Span<T>` through an internal `readonly ref struct` | Avoid ownership and slicing allocations; expose contiguous storage | `SortSpan` remains synchronous and stack-only |
| Comparer dispatch | `TComparer : IComparer<T>` is propagated as a concrete generic type | Permit value-type comparer specialization and avoid mandatory boxing/interface dispatch | Hot helpers must not erase it to `IComparer<T>` |
| Observation dispatch | `TContext : ISortContext` and value-type `NullContext` propagate through the full call chain | Allow the JIT to remove unobserved callback branches | A real context must receive every logical event |
| Primitive comparisons | Natural ordering specializes 13 primitive types through `typeof(T)` and `Unsafe.As` | Produce boolean comparisons; floating-point predicates include NaN ordering | Enabled only for `IComparableComparer`; custom comparers are never bypassed |
| Release element access | `MemoryMarshal.GetReference` and `Unsafe.Add(ref, (nint)(uint)index)` back `SortSpan` access. `Read`, `Write`, `Swap`, `IsElementLessThan` and `IsElementGreaterOrEqual` also take an `nint` index | Avoid repeated bounds checks and the sign-extension observed with an `int` index. An `int` index is zero-extended at each access, so a constant offset such as `i + 3` cannot fold into the address; an unrolled loop keeps its cursor in `nint` for that | Algorithm logic must establish valid indices. The `nint` overloads announce the same events as the `int` ones |
| Comparer-dependent termination | `OddEvenSort`, `CircleSort`, `GnomeSortNonOptimized`, `FunSort`, `BingoSort` and `CycleSort` count their passes, rounds or swaps against a bound that a consistent comparer never reaches | A comparer that is not a consistent total order cannot keep them running forever | `BogoSort` and `BozoSort` have no such bound, because a random shuffle has no worst case. `GnomeSort` needs none: with position memory every walk back ends at the front |
| Comparer-dependent cursors | In `QuadSort`, `FluxSort`, `CycleSort`, the unguarded core of `PairInsertionSort` and the sorts under `Algorithms/Partition`, a cursor or a write that only a consistent comparer keeps inside its range is also checked against the range. In the partition sorts and `PairInsertionSort`'s unguarded core, the checks inside loops drop out when `SortSpan.UsesNaturalPrimitiveOrder` holds | A comparer that is not a consistent total order cannot move unchecked access out of the buffer, and the natural primitive order, which cannot trip the checks, does not pay for them | The flag holds only for the internal natural comparer on the primitive set |
| Debug element access | Normal `Span<T>` indexing remains in Debug | Detect out-of-range algorithm defects during development | Debug and Release remain equivalent for valid input |
| Inlining | Small access, comparison, comparer, context, and utility methods use `AggressiveInlining` | Expose constants and generic types to callers and reduce hot call overhead when accepted by the JIT | Inlining is verified, not assumed |
| Local initialization | Module-level `SkipLocalsInit` | Avoid implicit clearing of locals and stack buffers that will be overwritten | Buffers read before overwrite explicitly `Clear` or `Fill` |
| Small temporary storage | Bounded metadata, count, recursion, and offset buffers use `stackalloc` | Avoid heap traffic for fixed or tightly bounded work memory | Review maximum byte count and stack depth per site |
| Large/generic storage | Algorithms rent from `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` | Reuse merge, tree, distribution, and work buffers | Return from `finally`; clear reference-containing arrays when required |
| Bit operations | `BitOperations.Log2` and `LeadingZeroCount` replace manual bit loops | Permit efficient platform lowering | Exact instructions depend on runtime and CPU |
| Bulk movement | `Span.CopyTo` performs overlap-safe range movement | Use the BCL's optimized generic copy rather than hand-written loops | Observable copies also account for logical reads/writes |
| Hot/cold shaping | Small hot helpers use `AggressiveInlining`; `IntroSortDotnet` marks its recursive core `NoInlining` | Balance specialization opportunities against caller code size | Applied locally from measurement or structural need |

The primitive set is `byte`, `sbyte`, `ushort`, `short`, `uint`, `int`, `ulong`, `long`, `nuint`, `nint`, `float`, `double`, and `Half`. Floating-point predicates preserve comparer ordering: NaN precedes numbers, NaNs compare equal, and signed zeros compare equal. Direct relational operators alone do not meet this contract.

InsertionSort prepares the NaN state of a cached key only after a shift is required, and reuses that state for the remaining comparisons. Already-ordered elements retain a short path. Other comparers and observing contexts retain their comparison results and event sequence. The [follow-up measurements](../reports/nan-comparison-optimization-2026-11-14.md) record the evidence; no prescan or different sorting algorithm is introduced.

### Why unchecked by-reference access is selective

RyuJIT already removes many bounds checks from simple forward loops through range analysis. Replacing every span access with `Unsafe` would therefore add risk without a guaranteed benefit. The retained `SortSpan` Release path was selected because one centralized implementation covers the irregular, backward, and runtime-indexed accesses where range proof is weakest, while Debug retains checked indexing.

The validation of unchecked access must cover irregular indices as well as sequential scans. Historical access-loop measurements and address-generation observations are kept in the [performance evidence record](../reports/performance-evidence-before-f03-2026-11-15.md).

The same validation rule applies to offset buffers in `PDQSortBranchless`: their store index is data-dependent, so each unchecked write needs a valid range established by the algorithm.

## Implemented Algorithm-Level Optimizations

### Branchless PDQSort partition

`PDQSortBranchless` is a scalar block-partition implementation, not an unimplemented SIMD proposal. It preserves PDQSort's pivot selection, duplicate handling, pattern detection, heapsort fallback, and tail-recursion elimination while replacing the data-dependent partition branch with two 64-byte offset buffers.

The partition preserves the following structure:

- boolean classification is converted with `Unsafe.As<bool, byte>` and accumulated into offset counts;
- runtime-indexed offset-buffer writes use first-element refs plus `Unsafe.Add` within the buffer bounds;
- classification is manually unrolled eight times, with its cursor and counts in `nint` so the constant offsets fold into the address;
- whole blocks of `int` keys in natural order, sorted without an observer, are classified by the sign of each key's 64-bit difference from the pivot and unrolled over the whole block. Other keys, comparers and observed sorts use the comparison form, and both store the same offsets;
- the block fills and the exchange are methods that are not inlined, and take the span by `in` and copy it to a local; and
- cyclic permutation exchanges misplaced pairs in blocks, reducing branch-predictor pressure on random and duplicate-heavy inputs.

The extra classification bookkeeping makes this a trade-off rather than a universal replacement for branchy PDQSort. Input predictability, size, runtime, and CPU affect the result. Measurements and crossover observations are kept in the [performance evidence record](../reports/performance-evidence-before-f03-2026-11-15.md).

### Branch reduction and guarded loops

The repository also applies branch-sensitive structure where an algorithm justifies it:

- `BlockQuickSort` classifies elements into block index buffers. Unconditional offset stores are confined to the `NullContext` path, because an observing context must not be told about index-buffer writes the algorithm did not logically perform;
- `Glidesort` contains branchless small sorting-network stages; its bidirectional stable partition uses a write-both kernel (unconditional stores to both candidate slots, the reference implementation's technique) and an AVX-512 compress kernel under `NullContext`, because RyuJIT compiles conditional-destination writes to data-dependent branches rather than cmov;
- `QuadSort` and `FluxSort` port quadsort's and fluxsort's branchless merge and partition steps in the reference's gcc form, which writes both candidates and advances the cursors arithmetically. The clang form selects the value to write, and RyuJIT compiled that selection inside the merge loop to a data-dependent branch (verified by disassembly), which made random input measurably slower. Unlike Glidesort the write-both form runs under every context, so observed counts describe the code the unobserved path runs;
- `InsertionSort` and `StdSort` use guarded/unguarded inner-loop variants where a sentinel or established boundary removes repeated boundary work;
- `StdSort` uses a natural-order primitive-type gate for 64-element bitset partitions and small conditional-move networks. Bitsets are local values. The gate does not depend on `TContext`, so observed statistics describe the same algorithm the fast path runs; classification state never touches an observable buffer;
- `HeapSort`, `MinHeapSort` and `BottomupHeapSort` pick the larger (or smaller) child by adding the comparison result to the index, as Rust's heapsort does, so the sift loop does not branch on the children's order. The comparisons, their order and every reported event stay the same. `float`, `double` and `Half` keep the branch, because their natural comparison branches on NaN internally. `TernaryHeapSort` keeps it too, because its second comparison needs the first one's winner; and
- PDQ variants use partial insertion-sort exits, already-partitioned detection, duplicate blocks, pattern-defeating shuffles, and heapsort fallback to avoid expensive work on favorable or adversarial inputs.

Branchless source syntax alone is not sufficient evidence. A ternary may still compile to a branch, and branch removal may increase instruction count or code size. The project validates relevant generated code and benchmarks multiple input patterns.

### Loop, recursion, and small-sort shaping

- Selected classification and copy loops are manually unrolled only when the JIT did not produce the desired shape and measurement justified it.
- Several quicksort and merge implementations use tail-recursion elimination or bounded explicit `stackalloc` work stacks to reduce call-stack growth and keep hot iteration local.
- Hybrid algorithms switch to insertion sort or sorting networks below algorithm-specific thresholds. Thresholds are local implementation decisions and do not define a package-wide constant.
- Cached pivot and element values reduce repeated observable reads and memory traffic.
- Distribution algorithms prefer shifts and masks for power-of-two radices and use compact count/offset buffers.

## Allocation And Memory Contract

- Hot element-processing loops do not perform per-element heap allocation.
- Bufferless algorithms remain bufferless apart from bounded stack or call metadata documented by the algorithm.
- Algorithms requiring generic auxiliary storage normally use `ArrayPool<T>`; pool misses and pool internals mean this is not a universal zero-allocation guarantee.
- Reference-containing rentals are returned with clearing where retention would be unsafe.
- `SkipLocalsInit` makes explicit initialization a correctness obligation. Histogram buffers that increment existing values are the highest-risk pattern and must be cleared before use.
- Generic `T` cannot generally be stack-allocated because it may contain references; metadata and generic element buffers use different strategies.

Allocation claims identify the algorithm, overload, element type, input size and pattern, runtime, and benchmark configuration.

## Benchmark And Disassembly Policy

Performance changes are evaluated in Release with BenchmarkDotNet. The repository harness:

- prepares fresh input buffers outside the measured region so a benchmark does not repeatedly sort an already-sorted array;
- generates each of an iteration's input buffers from its own seed, so no invocation of a seeded pattern sorts an input another invocation has already sorted (patterns that do not depend on a seed, such as sorted or pipe organ, are the same in every buffer by definition);
- pins invocation count to the prepared buffer count and uses `UnrollFactor=1`;
- records explicit tiering settings so runtime transitions do not silently change the measurement conditions; and
- uses a fixed CI CPU model unless explicitly overridden, improving comparability across runs.

| Claim | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Faster/slower or crossover point | BenchmarkDotNet across relevant sizes and patterns |
| Allocation reduction | `MemoryDiagnoser` allocated-byte results |
| Callback or generic branch removed | Disassembly of the closed `NullContext` specialization |
| `setcc`, `cmov`, bounds-check removal, unroll, instruction selection | `DisassemblyDiagnoser` output for the relevant hot method |
| Algorithmic complexity or stability | Implementation reasoning plus focused tests; microbenchmarks are insufficient |

A performance-sensitive change is compared with a meaningful baseline. Regressions require correction or an explicit documented trade-off. Benchmark noise and source-level intuition alone are not evidence.

### Evidence chain for retaining an optimization

Performance decisions follow the same reasoning chain used for the statistics counters and branchless PDQ partition:

1. state the expected bottleneck in CPU/JIT terms;
2. inspect closed-generic disassembly to confirm the expected costly or improved code shape;
3. compare before and after in the same benchmark run across relevant sizes and input classes;
4. verify that the result matches the hypothesis rather than an unrelated setup artifact;
5. run correctness, comparer, context, and allocation validation appropriate to the change; and
6. record the conditions where the choice wins, loses, and remains valid.

An optimization without this chain is a candidate, not an established project decision.

## Not Currently Adopted As Shared Infrastructure

The following are not repository-wide strategies: ISA-specific SIMD (`Vector128/256`, AVX, AdvSimd), portable `Vector<T>` sorting paths, `GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<T>`, `Unsafe.CopyBlock`, `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`, `Unsafe.BitCast`, and inline-array buffers. They remain outside the performance contract until correctness, portability, maintenance cost, generated code, and benchmarks justify adoption.

One local exception: `QuadSort` holds the 32-element stack array that quadsort's definition merges through (`VAR swap[32]` in the reference) in an `[InlineArray(32)]` struct of `T`, because `stackalloc` cannot hold an arbitrary generic `T`. The runtime tracks reference fields of an inline array, so the buffer is safe for reference-containing `T`; tests cover strings and records. It is the algorithm's own fixed-size stack storage, not shared infrastructure, and other algorithms do not reuse it.

## Non-goals

- Identical machine code across .NET versions, JIT modes, architectures, or NativeAOT
- A universal zero-allocation promise for every algorithm and context
- Making `StatisticsContext` safe for concurrent shared mutation
- Removing Debug bounds checks
- Bypassing a caller's comparer
- Replacing a BCL primitive merely because a lower-level API exists
- Requiring branchless execution where the branch predictor is faster

## Lessons Learned

- Generic `TContext` is essential: an interface-typed context prevents the unobserved path from specializing cleanly.
- Atomic statistics counters made observation disproportionately expensive; per-sort ownership enabled plain increments without weakening the intended usage model.
- Fresh input per benchmark invocation matters. Re-sorting one array trains predictors and can hide the advantage of branchless partitioning.
- A fresh copy of the same input is not fresh input. Until 2026-11-18 the harness copied one source array into every buffer. The predictor learned it across an iteration's 64 invocations, so branchy sorts on random data looked several times faster up to 4,096 elements (`PDQSort`: 29 µs at 4,096 and 202 µs at 8,192; with a seed per buffer, 108 µs and 234 µs). Watch for a jump between adjacent sizes far larger than n log n.
- Seed-independent patterns keep that bias, and pipe organ keeps it by choice. Measured on 2026-11-18 at 1,024 and 8,192 elements, branchy sorts ran faster on it than with an untrained predictor: `PDQSort` 1.7–2.3×, `PDQSortBranchless` 1.3–1.7×, `Span.Sort` 1.1–1.3×. Shifting the peak by ±32 removed most of the bias, but it also made `Span.Sort` 10–18% faster with an untrained predictor. The centered peak is what makes pipe organ a median-of-three worst case.
- Bounds-check removal matters most for irregular or runtime-indexed access. Simple forward loops are often already optimized by the JIT.
- Manual unrolling is justified only after disassembly shows the JIT did not unroll and benchmarks show an input-relevant benefit.
- Branchless classification helps unpredictable data but can lose on small or predictable inputs because extra bookkeeping remains.
- `SkipLocalsInit` turns an implicit runtime guarantee into a repository-wide audit obligation; increment-before-initialize buffers are easy to miss.
- A primitive fast path needs a natural-comparer marker. `typeof(T)` alone would silently violate reverse or domain-specific ordering.
- Generated code is a property of the closed generic instantiation, build configuration, JIT, and CPU; documentation describes the measured context.
- Preparing an invariant floating-point key can remove repeated NaN checks, but the measured element types and calling context determine whether it helps. Shared fallbacks need caller measurements as well as direct sort measurements. See the [2026-11-14 optimization record](../reports/prepared-floating-key-optimization-2026-11-14.md).
- Generic comparison policies can retain a common source loop. Helper boundaries and all shared callers still require correctness and performance validation.
- Type conditions that specialize to constants can still change inlining and code layout. Validate the generated code and all affected callers.
- Floating-point and integer measurements do not cover wider value types. Validate large structs separately before sharing a hot path.
- Before concluding two implementations have equivalent performance, include inputs that exercise their different work and memory traffic.
- Storing what a position already determines is a cost, not a safeguard. See the distribution auxiliary structure rule in `sorting_api.md`.
- A value select that RyuJIT turns into `cmov` outside a loop can still become a branch inside one. QuadSort's merge step was written as `dst = gt ? r : l`; outside the loop it compiled to `cmov`, inside the merge loop to `test`/`je`, and random input paid for the mispredictions (QuadSort at n = 100,000 random `int` went from 4.6 ms to 1.9 ms once the step wrote both candidates). Check the loop body, not the first unrolled step.
- A port that reproduces a reference's comparison counts exactly on identical inputs is the strongest fidelity evidence available for an adaptive sort, whose branching depends on the data. QuadSort and FluxSort were checked that way against the C sources, with the reference's address-derived sample offset replaced by the port's deterministic one. `ScandumReferenceTraceTests` keeps the check in the suite and compares the order of the compared pairs as well as their number, because sorted output cannot reveal a changed threshold or a skipped route.
- A port inherits the reference's trust in the comparer, but not the cost of breaking it. quadsort's cross merge and seven-element parity swap rely on earlier comparisons to keep their cursors inside the runs. So do the partition scans of the quicksort family and the unguarded insertion sorts that run on ranges with a sentinel before them, and the stable partitions that compare each element twice rely on the second pass repeating the first. With a comparer that is not a consistent total order, unchecked Release access ended the process with `AccessViolationException` in `PDQSort` and `IntroSort`, read outside the range in seven other partition sorts, copied memory from outside the span into `QuadSort`'s output, corrupted the heap through `StableQuickSort`'s scratch buffer, and left `BidirectionalStableQuickSort` partitioning without progress. These sorts now check those cursors and writes and throw `InvalidOperationException`. The checks compare indices and never elements, so comparison order is unchanged.
- Matching counts do not prove a partition holds the right elements. `BidirectionalStableQuickSort`'s second pass can fill its gap with exactly as many elements as the first pass skipped and still pick other ones, so a broken comparer can repeat some elements and lose others. Only recording the first pass's answers would prevent it, which the algorithm does not do, so the sort documents the loss instead. `StableQuickSort` writes every element exactly once in its second pass and keeps its elements.
- A probe of all 107 public sort classes with broken comparers (2026-11-19, Release, guard cells around the range, heap verification on) found two more that left their range. `PairInsertionSort` inserts the larger element of each pair without a bound and relies on the smaller one to stop it. `CycleSort`'s duplicate skip could end one place past the range. A consistent comparer stops that skip in time, because the cells from the item's position onward outnumber the copies of the item, but a deterministic comparer such as `x > y ? 0 : -1` does not. Ten classes could instead run forever while staying inside the range: `OddEvenSort`, `CircleSort`, both `GnomeSort` variants, `NaturalMergeSort`, `BogoSort`, `BozoSort` and `FunSort` stop only when their comparisons report order, `BingoSort`'s rounds place nothing when no element compares equal to the maximum, and `CycleSort`'s rotation need not return to its start. `BucketSortInteger` threw `IndexOutOfRangeException` from its bucket span, even for the consistent comparer that orders by absolute value, because it takes its minimum and maximum from the comparer and its buckets from the numeric values.
- A sort that repeats work until its comparisons report order can be bounded by its own theory instead of by a guess. The number of inversions bounds the swaps of `GnomeSort` and `FunSort` and the swapping passes of `CircleSort`. Odd-even transposition sorts within n phases, natural merge sort within ceil(log2 n) merge passes, cycle sort writes each element at most once and so rotates at most n steps in total, and `BingoSort` places an element in any two rounds in a row. Each bound costs a counter per pass, round, step or swap, and a consistent comparer never reaches it, so comparisons and results are unchanged. Every such counter folds away under the natural order of a primitive type, and the disassembly of the natural `int` sorts matched the old code apart from register names, one load outside a loop and, in `BingoSort`, the order of its blocks. With a custom struct comparer and `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0` (2026-11-19, 1,000 to 4,000 elements, up to 100,000 for the n log n and linear sorts), random input took 0.97 to 1.07 times the old time, the most for the per-swap counters of `FunSort`, `GnomeSortNonOptimized` and `GnomeSort` and the round counter of `BingoSort`. Other patterns ranged from 0.79 to 1.21 times, a spread that also appeared where no new instruction runs, such as `FunSort` on sorted input, which never reaches its counter. A counter taken once per outer step of `GnomeSort` instead of per swap cost sorted input up to 47%, because a sorted range takes an outer step for every comparison. `BucketSortInteger`'s check is the one comparison that also keeps its bucket index in range. Reaching it takes no longer than the algorithm's own worst case, except for `CircleSort`: no tighter bound on its passes is proven, and the inversion bound allows up to n(n - 1) / 2 of them. A random shuffle has no worst case, so `BogoSort` and `BozoSort` have no bound and still run forever with a comparer that never reports order.
- A cursor check inside a scan loop costs a compare and a branch for every element, and unrolling cannot remove it from the short scans of random input. PDQSort was timed under tiered compilation with the old and new code sorting the same inputs in one process (2026-11-19, 1,000 to 1,000,000 elements, median of per-input time ratios). With checks for every comparer, natural `int` sorts were 5–6% slower on random input and 9–15% slower on pipe-organ input. The natural order of a primitive type cannot trip the checks, so `SortSpan.UsesNaturalPrimitiveOrder` lets the JIT drop them there. Natural `int` and `double` sorts then stayed within the noise of an A/A control, in which two identical copies of the old code differed by up to 13% on sorted `double`. A custom struct comparer on `int` keeps the checks and was 3–5% slower on random input and 8–20% slower on pipe-organ input. IntroSort's new check is in its insertion sort, and it stayed within 5% with that comparer. The same timing of the nine other partition sorts that gained checks (1,000 to 100,000 elements, pipe-organ input only up to 10,000) kept natural `int` sorts between 0.83 and 1.07 times the old time, within that A/A noise. With the custom struct comparer, random input was up to 5% slower. Long scans cost the most: `QuickSort` on pipe-organ input took up to 1.31 times the old time and `IntroSortDotnet` on sorted input up to 1.27 times. `PairInsertionSort`'s check, timed the same way at 100 to 4,000 elements, left natural `int` sorts between 0.94 and 1.06 times the old time under tiered compilation and cost the custom struct comparer 2–5% at 1,000 and 4,000 elements with `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`.
- With `[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]` on the throw helper, the JIT kept the helper's call inside PDQSort's scan loop. The loop then took two branches per element and saved more registers. With `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, long scans took up to 1.38 times the old time. A plain `[DoesNotReturn]` helper let the JIT move the call to cold code after the method, which brought the worst case to 1.13 times.
- A guard cell catches a cursor that leaves a sliced span only on the high side. `SortSpan` widens the index as unsigned, so index -1 addresses about four billion elements past the start and faults before any guard cell is read. The safety tests therefore sort a range inside a larger span through the range overloads, which keeps guard cells on both sides within the span.
- PDQSort in C#, C++ and Rust was timed in one process on 2026-11-19: orlp's `pdqsort.h` built by MSVC and the pdqsort of the Rust standard library before 1.81 built by rustc, both loaded as DLLs and interleaved per input with the C# sorts (`int`, 1,000 to 1,000,000 elements, median of per-round ratios to MSVC's branchless build). A C# port written to orlp's structure made exactly the C++ comparison count in all 40 cases, so the gaps come from code generation, not from the algorithm. Branchy sorts are dominated by mispredictions: the C# ones took 1.03–1.09 times MSVC's branchy build. Insertion sort on 16 elements ran at MSVC's speed in `InsertionSort`. The block partition was the gap: one pass took about 1.5 times MSVC's time in `PDQSortBranchless`, and the whole sort 1.26–1.33 times on random input. Rust's pdqsort, which always partitions in blocks, ran within 6% of MSVC on random input, and g++ ran 3–10% faster than MSVC in separate processes.
- Three changes took `PDQSortBranchless` to 1.20–1.21 times MSVC's time on random input. Against the old code, random input took 0.90–0.96 times as long, few distinct values 0.89–0.92, reverse-sorted input 0.82–0.84 and pipe organ 0.91–0.95, and a custom struct comparer stayed between 0.80 and 1.00 on those patterns. `SortSpan` gained `nint` overloads, so the unrolled fills fold their constant offsets into the address. The fills and the exchange became methods that are not inlined; inlined again, reverse-sorted input took 8–12% longer. They take the span by `in` and copy it to a local. Passed by value, the caller copied the struct before each call, and a partition pass measured 2–5% slower than the old code. Read through the reference, the JIT reloaded the base pointer for every element, because the offset stores might alias it. orlp's newer block loop and 64-byte aligned offset buffers made no measurable difference. The order of announced operations did not change, and `PDQSortBranchlessTests` pins it at 1,000 elements.
- The classification step was the rest of the block partition gap, and C# matches MSVC on it for `int` keys. An earlier probe put the C# loop at 1.10–1.22 times MSVC's time, but its C++ kernel used a constant pivot of 0, which MSVC turned into a sign-bit extraction. With the pivot passed at run time, MSVC spends four ALU operations per element (`cmp`, `setcc`, the count `add` and the offset `lea`, after a `xor` that register renaming removes) and RyuJIT five, because every bool-to-integer form compiles to `setcc` and then `movzx`. Unrolling the whole block so that the stored offsets became constants made the fill 1.4–1.7 times slower on Zen 4. RyuJIT's `setcc` writes the low byte of a register that can still hold the previous count, and the `lea` that had overwritten that register was gone. The sign of an `int` key's 64-bit difference from the pivot needs no `setcc`. Unrolled over the whole block, it takes three ALU operations per element. The fills took 0.85–0.97 times the old time (MSVC 0.73–0.97), and one partition pass over 65,536 elements took 0.81 (MSVC 0.79). Summing two flags before adding them to the count changed nothing, so the count chain is not the limit (BenchmarkDotNet, .NET 11, `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, 2026-11-19).
- Matching MSVC in the partition pass moved the whole sort much less. In two paired runs of the old and new code with MSVC (`int`, 1,000 to 1,000,000 elements), random input took 0.95–1.01 times the old time, 16 distinct values 0.89–0.97 and reverse-sorted input 0.94–0.99. Random input stayed at about 1.2 times MSVC's time, so most of the remaining whole-sort gap is outside the block classification. Where it is has not been measured. The C++-shaped port stays at 1.14–1.16 times on the whole sort, and its insertion sort took 0.86–0.89 times MSVC's time on 16 elements.
- Interleaving implementations per input needs distance between their visits to the same input. When each implementation sorted the input that the previous one had just sorted, two copies of the same code differed by 7–27% at 1,000 elements, because code they share, such as `InsertionSort`, met branch history from the same data. Spacing the visits a third of the input pool apart brought that A/A ratio to 0.97–1.01.
- Recursion depth can match a reference while stack use does not, because a generic frame grows with the element. `FluxSort` recurses as deep as fluxsort, but tier-1 inlining put copies of 1 KiB elements into its partition frame, tens of kilobytes per level, and an input built to skew every partition overflowed the default stack at 1,000,000 elements with a valid comparer. Keeping element work out of the recursive method brought that frame to about 1 KB or less.

- The heap sorts were brought to the shape their definitions give them on 2026-11-20. `HeapSort`, `MinHeapSort` and `TernaryHeapSort` sift top-down in both phases, as Knuth's Algorithm H does, because descending to a leaf and climbing back up is `BottomupHeapSort`'s defining step and `HeapSort` had borrowed it for its build. `BottomupHeapSort` moves the maximum to the end and sifts from the root hole, as libstdc++'s `__pop_heap` does, instead of swapping. They were timed on random input of 1,000 to 100,000 elements (20,000 for `Half`, `decimal` and `string`), with the previous code interleaved in the same process, a fresh permutation for every sort and tiered compilation off. Over two runs, against the previous code, `HeapSort` and `MinHeapSort` took 0.67–0.71 times as long on `int`, 0.95–1.03 on `float` and `double`, 0.97–1.02 on `Half` and 0.97–1.07 on `decimal` and `string`. `BottomupHeapSort` took 0.63–0.70 on `int` and 0.89–1.00 on the other types. For binary heaps the bottom-up build was no faster than the top-down one. `TernaryHeapSort` became up to 10% slower with its top-down build (`int` 1.05–1.09, `float`, `double` and `Half` 1.03–1.10, `decimal` and `string` 0.95–1.04), which was accepted to keep it the plain d-ary heapsort.
- A second inlined copy of a hot loop can use up the JIT's inlining budget for everything else in the method. When `HeapSort`'s build began calling the extraction sift, both marked for aggressive inlining, `SortSpan.IsGreaterThan` (851 bytes of IL across its type branches) stayed a call for `float`, `double`, `Half`, `decimal` and `string`, and those sorts took 1.3–2.0 times as long while `int` was unaffected. `DOTNET_JitDisasmSummary` listed the helper as a separately compiled method. Moving the build into its own method restored them. Element types beyond `int` have to be measured after any change that inlines a loop twice.
- Adding a comparison result to an index removes a misprediction only when the comparison does not branch itself. The branchless child pick made the `int` heap sorts 0.63–0.72 times as long, but `float` and `double` took 1.10–1.13 times as long, because their natural comparison is `a > b || (IsNaN(b) && !IsNaN(a))`. For the ternary heap the arithmetic select took 1.20–1.29 times as long on `int`: the second comparison needs the first one's winner, so the select lengthens a chain of dependent loads.
- Halving the comparisons does not halve the time when comparisons are cheap. On 65,536 random `int` keys `BottomupHeapSort` makes 1.02 n log₂ n comparisons against `HeapSort`'s 1.81 n log₂ n. It takes 0.63–0.66 times `HeapSort`'s time on culture-sensitive `string` keys, but 1.07–1.17 times on `int`, where the climb's extra moves outweigh the saved comparisons.
- The remaining heap-family sorts were checked against their definitions the same day, with the same timing method. `WeakHeapSort` holds the new root element in a local while it merges with each node of the distinguished path, so a merge that moves an element writes once instead of swapping, and its final swap is unconditional as in the definition. `PoplarHeapSort`'s sift moves elements through a hole. On 1,204 inputs each, both compared the same pairs in the same order as the previous code, except the final comparison `WeakHeapSort` no longer makes. Over two runs `WeakHeapSort` took 0.86–0.90 times as long on `int`, `float` and `double` and 0.90–1.05 on `Half`, `decimal` and `string`; `PoplarHeapSort` took 0.91–0.97 and 0.93–1.03.
- `TournamentSort` used to write its output in place. That moved a still-competing element into the winner's slot, so every extraction replayed a second path, and random input took 1.39–1.48 n log₂ n comparisons where tree selection needs at most n log₂ n. With the separate output area of the definition, each extraction replays one path, and the sort took 0.56–0.68 times as long on every element type measured. A tie goes to the left contestant, which holds the earlier element, so this form is also stable: `IsStable` became true, and the winners are written to buffer 2.
- The four textbook merge sorts were checked against their definitions on 2026-11-20. None runs a stage outside merge sort, but each did work its definition does not need. On 10,000 random `int` keys `NaturalMergeSort` made 271,089 comparisons, 2.1 times `MergeSort`'s, because it found its runs again before every pass, as tape-era natural merging does. Detecting the runs once and merging the recorded boundaries, with one comparison to skip a pair already in order, brought that to 136,559. Buffering only the shorter run of each merge, as Rust's slice merge and libstdc++'s `__merge_adaptive` do, took 10,000 keys, sorted except for 100 random ones at the end, from 124,627 comparisons and 119,704 writes to 63,876 and 54,177; the rest of the gap to `MergeSort`'s 21,033 and 21,389 is the fixed pairing, which merges the long run on every pass. The pass count no longer depends on the comparer, so the pass counter added on 2026-11-19 is gone. `PingpongMergeSort` copied each leaf element from source to destination although the bootstrap had already put it in both buffers, n reads and n writes that changed nothing. All four read both heads at every merge step; keeping the head that was not taken in a local cut the index reads of random input by 34% in `MergeSort` and 40% in `BottomupMergeSort`, at unchanged comparisons.
- Timed against the previous code in one process (`DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, 1,000 to 100,000 elements, median of 11 to 31 interleaved rounds), `NaturalMergeSort` took 0.68–0.76 times as long on random `int` and `double` keys, 0.46–0.54 on `string`, and 0.40–0.62 on nearly sorted input of all three. `MergeSort`, `BottomupMergeSort` and `PingpongMergeSort` took 0.88–0.98 on random `int` and `double`; on `string`, where comparisons dominate, they stayed within 0.92–1.09, the run-to-run spread. `PingpongMergeSort` took 0.83–0.90 on sorted `int` and `double`. Writing `runEnd++` inside the argument of the run's first comparison made RyuJIT add a register copy to the ascending scan and leave the loop unaligned, and sorted `int` and `double` took 1.06–1.27 times as long; with the increment in each branch the loop matched the old one instruction for instruction and the time returned to 0.99.
- The rotate merge sorts were brought to libstdc++'s `__inplace_stable_sort` the same day. Their insertion-sort leaves had been 16 elements with no source; libstdc++ insertion-sorts ranges shorter than 15, so `RotateMergeSortRecursive` and `RotateMergeSortNonOptimized` now stop dividing at 14 elements and `RotateMergeSort` seeds 14-element blocks. `RotateMergeSort` and `RotateMergeSortRecursive` also rotated a pair in one step when every element of its left run exceeded every element of its right run. Neither Dudziński and Dydek's merge nor libstdc++'s `__merge_without_buffer` has that step, and its stated purpose was to take reversed input out of the merge's worst case, which the definition keeps. On 10,000 `int` keys, removing it raised the comparisons of reversed input from 76,248 to 91,214 bottom-up and from 45,966 to 81,561 recursive and about doubled its writes, while random input fell from about 254,000 to 216,000 comparisons, because the step cost one per merge decision. Timed as above (`int`, 1,000 to 100,000 elements), reversed input took 2.9 times as long bottom-up and 3.7–5.1 times recursive, few distinct values 1.21–1.44 times, and random input 1.03–1.06 bottom-up and 1.10–1.20 recursive. `RotateMergeSortRecursive` now compares exactly as often as `RotateMergeSortNonOptimized`, which tests pin. At 10,000 and 100,000 elements, where the leaf sizes did not change, its sorted input took 1.19–1.53 times as long as before and the same time as `RotateMergeSortNonOptimized`; the instructions it executes there are the same as before apart from register names, so that gap is code placement, not work.
- The modern merge sorts were checked against their reference sources the same day. `PowerSort`, `TimSort` and `ShiftSort` now reproduce the comparison trace of their C++ sources exactly on every shape and size of `MergeReferenceTraceTests` (sandbox/MergeReferenceTrace/trace.cpp prints the rows). Each had drifted in one place: `TimSort` extended runs with a binary insertion that first compared an element with its predecessor, which CPython's binarysort does not (random input took 127,216 comparisons instead of 119,849 at 10,000 `int` keys); `PowerSort` insertion-sorted inputs shorter than its minimum run without looking for a run (20 reversed keys took 190 comparisons instead of 20); and `ShiftSort` split its derivative list without the reference's gap. The gap split makes two merges per node and merges the gap sublist into the right half first; it took 1.22 times the comparisons on random input and 1.59 on reversed input at 10,000 keys, 0.87 on nearly sorted input, and `string` sorts took 1.15–1.60 times as long.
- `SpinSort` sorted inputs of up to 72 elements by binary insertion where Boost's spinsort uses linear insertion. `FlatStableSort`'s range sorts called each other and insertion-sorted 32-element leaves before copying them, where Boost's `internal_sort` goes one level deeper so that every leaf is sorted where its elements already are; following Boost cut the comparisons of 1,000 random `int` keys from 13,337 to 10,286 and the writes from 14,368 to 10,397. `Glidesort`'s pivot took one level of median-of-three where the reference recurses to about n^0.528 samples, and its tail blocks were insertion-sorted where the reference sorts power-of-two blocks with its networks; four of its merges also carried an already-sorted check the reference does not have, which never fired on random or few-distinct input. Timed against the previous code (median of 21 interleaved rounds), `Glidesort` took 1.02–1.03 times as long on random `int` keys and up to 1.11 on 10,000 keys with 16 distinct values, all of it from the recursive pivot.
- `Driftsort`'s bidirectional merge and `Glidesort`'s symmetric merges let a comparer that is not a consistent total order repeat some elements and lose others, because they did not check that the forward and backward cursors meet. The references check it; `Driftsort` now copies its input back and throws, `Glidesort` copies its input back and continues as its reference does, and both are in `InconsistentComparerSafetyTests`.
- `SmoothSort`'s summary claimed about 1.5 n log n comparisons on average. It makes 2.56 n log₂ n on 65,536 random `int` keys and 1.97 on reversed ones, because a Leonardo tree is about 1.44 times as deep as a binary heap of the same size and a sift compares twice per level. The code was not changed.
- The insertion sorts were checked against their definitions on 2026-11-20 (counts on 1,000 `int` keys). `PairInsertionSort` inserted the smaller element of each pair and then the larger one from the top of the prefix, two straight insertions after an extra comparison: 499,999 comparisons on reversed input against straight insertion's 499,500. It now inserts the larger element first, moving every element above it two places, and continues the smaller one from where the larger stopped, as JDK 7's `DualPivotQuicksort` does: 250,499 comparisons on reversed input and 163,733 on random input, against 243,796 for straight insertion, with writes falling alike. `GnomeSort` claimed position memory but stepped back up over the pairs it had just ordered, so it made exactly the comparisons of `GnomeSortNonOptimized`; returning to the remembered position saves one comparison per swap (486,600 to 243,796 on random input) and ends every walk at the front, so its swap budget is gone. `BinaryInsertionSort` compared each element with its predecessor before searching, which binary insertion does not; sorted input now takes Σ⌊log₂(i+1)⌋ comparisons (7,987) instead of 999. The Shell sorts exchanged neighbours along each chain; holding the element as Knuth's Algorithm D does keeps every comparison and cut the writes of random input from 18,076 to 12,424 and its reads from 46,282 to 19,560 in `ShellSortKnuth1973`.
- Timed against the previous code in one process (`DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, median of 15 interleaved rounds, `int`, `double` and `string`, 256 to 100,000 elements), `PairInsertionSort` took 0.48–0.66 times as long on reversed input and 0.66–0.94 on random input, `GnomeSort` 0.43–0.49 on `int`, 0.66–0.74 on `double` and 0.50–0.57 on `string`, and the Shell sorts 0.78–1.00 on `int`, 0.55–0.86 on `double` and 0.98–1.07 on `string`. `BinaryInsertionSort` took 5–18 times as long on sorted input, the cost of searching every element, 0.93–1.5 on nearly sorted input and 0.89–1.02 on random and reversed input. Testing after a scan whether it moved anything made sorted and reversed `int` Shell sorts 1.2–1.6 times slower than the exchanges, and sorted `int` pair insertion 1.4 times slower; comparing with the element below first and shifting only when it is greater, as libc++ and Rust insert a tail, removed both.
- Not adopted, because the definitions do not contain them: libstdc++'s insertion sort compares each element with the first one and moves the whole prefix when it is smaller, which makes sorted input cost 2(n - 1) comparisons; JDK 7 skips the ascending prefix before it starts pairing; and the random insertion order of Bender, Farach-Colton and Mosteiro's library sort would give up `LibrarySort`'s stability.
- The distribution sorts were checked against their definitions on 2026-11-20. `CountingSort`, `PigeonholeSort`, the LSD and MSD radix sorts, `RotateLSDRadixSort` and `Radsort` were left as they were. `FlashSort` computed each class as an exact `UInt128` product divided by the key span, a 128-bit division in software, and classifies every element at least twice. Neubert's Flashsort1 multiplies by the floating-point constant c1 = (m - 1) / (max - min) instead, which keeps classes in range and in key order, and with it `FlashSort` took 0.30–0.41 times as long on random `int` keys and 0.17–0.18 on sorted and nearly sorted ones (1,024 to 65,536 elements). A closed cycle also no longer re-reads the element it has just written to classify it again.
- `BucketSort` and `BucketSortInteger` divided each key distance by an integer bucket width ⌈range / k⌉. Just above range = n that width is 2, so only half the buckets could receive an element. They now use the textbook ⌊k × distance / range⌋, computed as one multiplication by k / range in double: an exact 64-bit division per element instead made `BucketSortInteger` take 1.23–1.68 times as long on sorted input at 8,192 and 65,536 elements, where the old width was 1. With the multiplication, `BucketSortInteger` took 0.84–0.96 times as long on every pattern and `BucketSort.SortBy` 0.83–1.02. On 10,000 keys drawn from [0, 15,000) the comparisons inside the buckets fell from 5,258 to 4,463.
- `AmericanFlagSort` exchanged each misplaced element with the slot it belongs in and read the leader slot again. It now carries the evicted element in a local around the cycle, as McIlroy, Bostic and McIlroy's program does, and writes the leader slot once when the cycle closes. The permutation is the same, but the same 10,000 keys took 49,999 reads and 19,936 writes instead of 88,955 reads and 38,956 writes. On `int` keys the time stayed between 0.94 and 1.05 times the old, and through a key selector it was 0.90–0.93. `SpreadSort` takes the key extremes of the ordered prefix from its two ends, as Boost's `is_sorted_or_find_extremes` does, instead of scanning the prefix again: 0.88–0.91 times as long on nearly sorted input, and unchanged elsewhere. All of these were timed against the previous code in one process (`DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, median of 36 to 360 interleaved rounds).
- `AmericanFlagSort` stops the permutation before the last occupied bucket, as the paper's Program 4.2 does. It used to stop only before bucket 255. Once the buckets below the last occupied one are full, that bucket's range holds only its own elements. Reads fall only by the tail of that bucket that no cycle reached: 17 of 49,961 on 10,000 sorted keys, and none on shuffled keys, whose cycles read nearly every slot of it while carrying elements in. The time gain comes from the small inner levels instead, which now stop scanning the 256 counters at the last occupied bucket, both in the uniform-digit check and in the permutation. On random full-range `int` keys the time was 0.75–0.81 of the previous version at 256 to 65,536 elements, and on 40 distinct values it was 0.43 at 256 elements, 0.59–0.61 at 1,024, and 0.89–0.99 at 8,192 and 65,536. Every other pattern stayed within 0.90–1.04 (two runs, median of 60 to 600 interleaved rounds, `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`).
- Not adopted for `AmericanFlagSort`: ska_sort's round-based partitioning and Boost's 3-way swap, because each defines another algorithm. The small-pile insertion sort, which the MSD radix sorts and `AmericanFlagSort` dropped on 2026-11-16, is not adopted either. McIlroy, Bostic and McIlroy keep it out of the plain programs: their two-array sort (Program 3.1) and in-place permutation (Program 4.1) have no cutoff, and the paper calls the versions that add one hybrid (Program B, and Program C, "Hybrid American flag sort", threshold 16). ArrayV's American flag and MSD radix sorts have none either.
- The selection sorts were checked against their definitions on 2026-11-20. `BingoSort` already followed the Wikipedia pseudocode and `SelectionSort` the textbook scan, and both were left as they were. `DoubleSelectionSort` compared every element with both the minimum and the maximum, 2(k - 1) comparisons for a pass over k elements. The bidirectional variant as Wikipedia defines it, and the way CLRS §9.1 and C++ `std::minmax_element` find both extremes, compares each pair once and then only its smaller element with the minimum and its larger with the maximum: ⌈3k/2⌉ - 2 comparisons, 374,750 instead of 500,000 on 1,000 keys. It also takes the first smallest key as the minimum and the last largest as the maximum, `std::minmax_element`'s tie rule, so a region of equal keys no longer swaps twice per pass.
- On random input the pair comparison is a branch that mispredicts about half the time. For types whose natural comparison does not branch, `DoubleSelectionSort` picks the pair's smaller and larger index by adding the comparison result, as `HeapSort` picks a child, and reads both elements again for their candidate comparisons. `float`, `double` and `Half` keep the branch, because their natural comparison branches on NaN internally. Timed against the previous code, `int` took 0.65–0.87 times as long (1.02 on 256 keys with 16 distinct values), `string` 0.73–0.81, `decimal` 0.80–1.02 and `Half` 0.73–1.00. `float` and `double` took 0.43–0.84 on sorted and reversed input but 1.09–1.57 on random and 16-distinct-value input: the previous code tested each element against both candidates through two well-predicted branches, and the definition puts one unpredictable branch per pair in their place. Merging the two outcomes of that branch into shared locals before the candidate comparisons made the floating-point form slower still, 1.5–2.0 on the same inputs; comparing inside each branch avoids it.
- `CycleSort`'s summary claimed n(n - 1)/2 comparisons on every input. That holds only when nothing moves: every element placed after a cycle's first costs another count over the rest of the range, so reversed input takes about 1.75 times as many and one cycle through every element about three times as many. Its count now adds each comparison result instead of branching on it, inside a prepared-key loop so that a floating-point item resolves its NaN state once. Without the prepared key, the branchless count made `double` and `float` 1.1–1.7 times slower, because their natural comparison branches on NaN. The new count reproduces the previous event streams and element bits in `PreparedFloatingSortEventTests`. Timed against the previous code, random and 16-distinct-value input took 0.60–0.73 times as long on `int`, 0.47–0.57 on `float` and `double` and 0.84–0.95 on `Half`; sorted input 0.84–1.04; `decimal` and `string` stayed within the noise of an unchanged anchor sort; reversed `int`, whose branch predicted well, took 1.08–1.11.
- `PancakeSort` flips with `MemoryExtensions.Reverse` when nothing observes it, which the runtime vectorizes for primitive types, and keeps one swap per exchanged pair when observed. On random and 16-distinct-value input it took 0.65–0.73 times as long on `int`, 0.70–0.82 on `float` and `double`, 0.90–0.92 on `Half` and 0.90–1.01 on `decimal`; sorted and reversed input, which flips at most once, and `string` stayed within the anchor's noise. Holding the scan's candidate by value instead of by index was tried for `SelectionSort` and `PancakeSort` and dropped: `int` did not change and `double` gained about 10%, but on sorted input, where the maximum changes at every element, `Half` and `decimal` took 1.11–1.14 times as long, and libc++'s `min_element` and Rust's `min_by` keep an iterator or a reference, not a copy.
- Timings in these selection-family entries: one process, `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, median of 21 interleaved rounds against renamed copies of the previous code, 256 and 1,024 elements, random, sorted, reversed and 16-distinct-value input, with the unchanged `BingoSort` as anchor; it varied 0.76–1.15 between identical copies.
- The tree sorts were checked against their definitions on 2026-11-20, and all seven follow them. Only two code changes came out of it. `TreapSort` announced a read of the inserted node's priority at every heap-up level and once more after the loop, although it holds the priority from its first read. `CartesianTreeSort` popped the minimum by moving the last queue entry to the top, and then pushed each child. Now one child takes the minimum's place at the top and is sifted down, and only the other child is pushed: the replace-top of Rust's `BinaryHeap::peek_mut` and Python's `heapreplace`. The sifted node is held while the others move, as in Rust's `Hole`, so its value is read once per sift. The extraction order does not change, because the queue orders by value and then by position, which is a total order. On 4,096 keys, extraction took 16.3n comparisons instead of 17.9n on random input, and 2.5n instead of 12.4n on sorted input with n/64 random exchanges. Announced reads fell by 25% on 16,384 random keys. Timed against the previous code: random input 0.90–0.96, 16 distinct values 0.88–0.97, nearly sorted input 0.23–0.62. Path-shaped input (sorted, reversed, pipe organ), where extraction compares nothing, measured 0.78–1.11.
- Not adopted for the tree sorts. A bottom-up sift for the Cartesian queue (libstdc++ `__adjust_heap`, Rust `sift_down_to_bottom`) cut comparisons on random input by 33–39% and took 0.60–0.65 as long on random `string` keys. But it always descends to the bottom, so nearly sorted input took only 0.67–0.99 as long, against 0.23–0.62 for the top-down replacement, and the adaptivity is the reason the sort exists. Moving the smaller child to the top, at one more comparison, saved 15% of the comparisons on 16 distinct values and none on random keys. Branch-free child selection in `BinaryTreeSort`'s descent (`Left` or `Right` picked by the sign of the comparison) took 1.05–1.31 times as long, because the descent is a chain of dependent loads and a predicted branch lets the next load start early. The branch-free loop of Rust's `binary_search_by`, used for `BTreeSort`'s in-node search, took 1.03–1.73 times as long and costs one more comparison on a full 15-key node.
- Timings in these tree-family entries: one process, `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, median of 11 interleaved rounds against renamed copies of the previous code, with fresh inputs in every round; `int`, `double`, `string` and `decimal`; 1,024 and 16,384 elements.
- The partition sorts were checked against their definitions on 2026-11-20. `PDQSort` and `PDQSortBranchless` ran a stage pdqsort.h does not have: after each partition they grew a block of keys equal to the pivot around it, left the block out of the recursion and judged balance without it, which also moved the bad-partition threshold. Their guarded first scans also skipped the one comparison pdqsort.h makes where the cursors meet. Without both, they reproduce the comparison count and the compared pairs of orlp's pdqsort.h on every row of `PdqReferenceTraceTests` (sandbox/PdqReferenceTrace/trace.cpp, 180 cases); before, they matched it only on inputs without repeated keys. The hash there is a sum because the C# recurses on the smaller side and pdqsort on the left; each side sees the same range and budget either way. `PDQSortBranchless` took 1.06–1.10 times as long on `int` keys with 16 distinct values and 0.94–1.03 elsewhere; `PDQSort` 0.88–1.04.
- `IntroSort` combined .NET's threshold and depth limit, the median-of-5 and nearly-sorted exit of libc++ at 368faac and a quartile pivot of its own. It now follows Musser's paper: the median value of the first, middle and last elements, the HP STL's unguarded partition, a depth limit of 2⌊log₂ n⌋, recursion on the right part, and one insertion sort over the whole range once every part holds 16 or fewer elements. Without the nearly-sorted exit, sorted, reversed and pipe-organ input took 2.0–6.1 times as long; random input took 0.91–1.05 and 16 distinct values 0.84–1.00.
- `DualPivotQuickSort` cited Yaroslavskiy's 2009 paper but used Java 7's five-sample pivots and threshold of 47. It now follows the paper: pivots at left + len/div and right − len/div with div starting at 3 and growing after a center of fewer than 13 elements, insertion sort below len = 27, and the paper's pass for elements equal to the pivots. On 100,000 random `int` keys it makes 1.26 n log₂ n comparisons, approaching the paper's 1.9 n ln n ≈ 1.32 n log₂ n from below, instead of 1.29 with the five samples. Times were 0.87–1.11, except sorted input of 1,024 elements, 1.28–1.30.
- `DestswapStableQuickSort` became a plain stable quicksort around glidesort's destination-swap partition, by the user's decision: the bottom-up merge sort for ranges below 16 and after 2 log₂ n levels is gone, the pseudo-median recurses as glidesort's `median3_rec` does, and the less side keeps the ancestor pivot. Its worst case is O(n²) again. Comparisons on 100,000 random keys rose from 1.10 to 1.33 n log₂ n and on sorted keys from 0.89 to 1.28; it took 1.16–1.39 times as long on random input, 1.3–2.1 on sorted input and 0.83–1.08 on 16 distinct values. A comparer that keeps a partition from shrinking makes it leave that range unsorted rather than throw, because elements of other ranges may still be in scratch.
- `BidirectionalStableQuickSort` claimed one pass but found the equal elements with a second scan that compared every element again, and reversed the greater section with swaps. Equal elements now move to the front of the range during the scan, and the greater section is reversed while it is copied back, as driftsort's `stable_partition` does. On 100,000 random keys it makes 1.70 n log₂ n comparisons instead of 3.32, no swaps instead of 0.25 n log₂ n, and 2.34 n log₂ n reads instead of 3.90; it took 0.50–0.85 times as long. Every element is written to one place, so the range keeps its elements under a broken comparer too. `StableQuickSort` holds the pivot and compares the element it has already read by value, which cut its reads from 6.44 to 3.38 n log₂ n; times 0.90–1.09.
- `StdSort` fell back to `HeapSort`'s top-down heapsort where libc++ calls `__partial_sort`: `__make_heap` with a held hole, then `__sort_heap`, whose pop runs Floyd's sift down to a leaf and a sift up. It now carries that heap. Pipe-organ input sends 77–93% of 16,384 and 131,072 elements to the fallback, and there `int` first took 1.55 times as long; adding the larger-child comparison to the index, as `HeapSort` does, brought it to 1.11–1.12 (`double`, which keeps the branch, 1.05–1.15), the cost of the climb's extra moves already seen for `BottomupHeapSort`. Other patterns stayed within the anchor's noise. `Ipnsort`'s bidirectional merges now check that their cursors meet and restore the input before reporting the comparer, as the reference and `Driftsort` do.
- Not changed in this pass: `BlockQuickSort` differs from the reference's `blocked_double_pivot_check_mosqrt` (it partitions the pivot sample again, uses its own duplicate-check conditions and a depth limit two levels lower, heapsorts small ranges at the limit, and swaps where the reference rotates through a hole); its re-port was deferred by the user and its summary lists the differences. `StdSort`'s guarded partition scans still skip a few comparisons whose result is known and that libc++ makes. `SampleSort` re-samples exhausted ranges as CPython's samplesort did; Frazer and McKellar's paper was not available to check.
- Timings in these partition-family entries: one process, `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, median of 11 interleaved rounds against renamed copies of the previous code, fresh inputs in every round; `int` and `double` at 1,024, 16,384 and 131,072 elements and `string` at 1,024 and 16,384; random, 16 distinct values, sorted, reversed, nearly sorted and pipe organ. An unchanged `QuickSort` timed against itself varied 0.93–1.08.

## Compiler-Specific Reporting Helper Inlining

The four observed-comparison reporting helpers in `SortSpan` request aggressive inlining only when compiled with `NETWASM`. NetWasm SDK 0.13.0 supplies that symbol automatically. Standard .NET builds retain the compiler's existing inlining heuristics. The condition changes method implementation hints, not comparisons, callback ordering, buffer identities, or bounds checks.

Compiler-specific measurements and rejected alternatives are retained in the [performance evidence record](../reports/performance-evidence-before-f03-2026-11-15.md). They do not promise the same behavior on another runtime or compiler.

A consumer must build the library sources with the NetWasm SDK to obtain these hints; consuming an ordinary precompiled .NET assembly does not retroactively apply the condition. Do not define `NETWASM` for the standard .NET browser runtime merely to force these hints. Revalidate this compiler-specific decision when upgrading the runtime or changing the call/recording path.
